articles.title: The Last Man Into the Stadium
articles.dek: In 1968 an injured runner limped into a nearly empty Olympic stadium more than an hour after the race was won. Hebrews 12 shows why that is how faith finishes.
articles.quote: The people who finish the race become the witnesses who help someone else finish theirs.
articles.body:
On the evening of October 20, 1968, the Olympic stadium in Mexico City was emptying. The marathon had ended more than an hour earlier, when Mamo Wolde of Ethiopia crossed the line in just over two hours and twenty minutes. The medals had been awarded, the anthems played, and the sun had gone down behind the stands. Most of the crowd had already gathered their things and gone home, and the few thousand who stayed were heading for the gates when word came from the tunnel that one more runner was still on the course.

His name was John Stephen Akhwari, and he ran for Tanzania. Somewhere in the race, as runners jostled for position, he had gone down hard. His knee was badly cut and dislocated, and his shoulder had struck the pavement. Medical staff bandaged him and expected him to quit. He got up instead, and for mile after mile he limped through the thin air of a city more than two thousand meters above the sea. Many healthy runners had already dropped out and gone back to their hotels.

When he finally came into the stadium, his leg wrapped and bloodied, the people still there began to cheer. They rose and applauded him around the last lap as if he had won. He crossed the line in three hours, twenty-five minutes, the last of fifty-seven finishers. Afterward someone asked him why he had kept going with no hope of a medal. Akhwari answered quietly: “My country did not send me 5,000 miles to start the race. My country sent me 5,000 miles to finish the race.”

The Letter to the Hebrews was written to people who were tempted to stop running. Its first readers were Jewish believers in Jesus who had started well. In their early days they stood their ground in a great conflict full of suffering, endured public insult, stood by friends in prison, and “joyfully accepted the confiscation of your property” (Hebrews 10:34). Years passed, though, and the pressure did not lift. The familiar world of the synagogue looked safer than the hard road of following a crucified Messiah. The writer's great fear is that they will slowly “drift away” (Hebrews 2:1) or “shrink back” (Hebrews 10:39).

So in chapter 11 he reads them a roll call of faith. Abel, Noah, Abraham, Sarah, Moses, Rahab, and a crowd of unnamed believers who were mocked, flogged, chained, and driven into caves all pass before our eyes. Then comes a surprising line: “These were all commended for their faith, yet none of them received what had been promised” (Hebrews 11:39). They ran their whole lives toward a finish line they never saw. With that line still ringing in their ears, the readers turn the page and find themselves standing in a stadium.

“Therefore, since we are surrounded by such a great cloud of witnesses, let us throw off everything that hinders and the sin that so easily entangles. And let us run with perseverance the race marked out for us, fixing our eyes on Jesus, the pioneer and perfecter of faith. For the joy set before him he endured the cross, scorning its shame, and sat down at the right hand of the throne of God.” (Hebrews 12:1–2)

Many of us picture that cloud of witnesses as spectators in the stands, peering down to judge how we are doing. The Greek word is martys, a person who gives testimony in court, the same word that later gave us “martyr.” One way to read the image is that the heroes of chapter 11 surround us as a body of evidence. Each of their lives says the same thing: the course can be finished, and God keeps faith with people who keep going.

The words for the race are just as honest. “Race” translates agōn, the root of our English word “agony,” the term for an athletic contest that demanded everything a person had. “Perseverance” is hypomonē, which pictures someone remaining under a heavy load without setting it down. The writer never pretends the race is short or easy. He does say it is “marked out for us,” a course God has set before each of his children, which means your stretch of road is yours to run and no one else's. He also tells us to throw off “everything that hinders.” The word there, onkos, means bulk or excess weight, and ancient runners raced with almost nothing on. Some of what slows us down is sin, and some of it is simply extra weight: a grudge we keep rehearsing, a worry we carry to bed every night, a habit that steals the hours we need for rest and prayer.

“Fixing our eyes” comes from a verb that means to look away from everything else and toward a single point. That point is Jesus, called the archēgos, the pioneer who goes first and cuts the trail, and the teleiōtēs, the one who carries a thing through to its finish. He ran this course ahead of us, all the way through the cross, and he finished. He endured because he kept his eyes on “the joy set before him,” the joy of a family redeemed and brought home. That is why the writer adds, “Consider him who endured such opposition from sinners, so that you will not grow weary and lose heart” (Hebrews 12:3).

The verses that follow explain the painful stretches of the course. “Endure hardship as discipline; God is treating you as his children” (Hebrews 12:7). The word for discipline, paideia, was the everyday word for raising and training a child. A coach pushes the athlete he believes in, and a father trains the son he loves. The writer admits that “no discipline seems pleasant at the time, but painful,” and then promises that “later on, however, it produces a harvest of righteousness and peace for those who have been trained by it” (Hebrews 12:11).

Then the passage closes with a picture that is easy to rush past. “Therefore, strengthen your feeble arms and weak knees. ‘Make level paths for your feet,’ so that the lame may not be disabled, but rather healed” (Hebrews 12:12–13). The writer is weaving together Isaiah 35:3 and Proverbs 4:26, and the runner he describes at the end of this great chapter is tired and limping. He also has someone else in view. The reason to make your path level is so that the lame runner coming behind you can make it too. This suggests that the Christian race is run in company, and that how steadily you run shapes the ground for the wounded person following in your steps.

That turns the cloud of witnesses into something that keeps growing. Abraham and Rahab testify to us, and in time our own faithfulness testifies to the people behind us. John Stephen Akhwari finished last, yet his limp around that final lap has been retold to generations of young athletes who wanted to quit. The man nobody waited for became a witness. The people who finish the race become the witnesses who help someone else finish theirs.

You may be running hurt right now. Perhaps you are an OFW counting the months to the next trip home, a parent caring for a sick spouse through long nights, a student preparing to retake a board exam, or a believer whose prayers seem to echo in an empty stadium. Hebrews does not ask you to run fast. It asks you to keep moving, to set down one weight you have been carrying for no good reason, and to lift your eyes to the One who has already crossed the line and is waiting for you there. This week you might read Hebrews 12:1–3 each morning before you check your phone, and then think of one person limping a little behind you and send them a message, bring them a meal, or simply sit with them for an hour.

God sent you into this race to finish it, and Jesus has already run every mile of it ahead of you. Whatever your pace today, keep going toward him. Someone behind you is watching how you run, and your steady, limping faithfulness may be the very thing that helps them home.

articles.title: The Love That Remembered
articles.dek: Ezekiel 16 tells the story of an unwanted baby, a broken covenant, and a God who would not forget. Its final verses are among the most tender lines in the whole book.
articles.quote: The love that found you before you could do anything is the same love that remembers you after you have done everything wrong.
articles.body:
In delivery rooms around the world, nurses now do something that would have seemed odd a generation ago. When a newborn's temperature begins to drop, they often lay the baby, skin against skin, on the mother's bare chest and cover them both with a blanket. Researchers who studied this practice, often called kangaroo care, found something remarkable. Nursing scientist Susan Ludington-Hoe and others reported that the skin over a mother's breast warmed when a chilled infant was placed there, and cooled again as the baby grew too warm, shifting by as much as a degree or two Celsius. Scientists call it thermal synchrony, and it happens without the mother deciding anything at all.

The baby contributes nothing to this. A newborn cannot ask for warmth or earn it, and it does not even know that it is cold. It simply lies there, and the body that loves it reads its need and answers. Any Filipino mother or lola who has held a shivering infant close during a long brownout already understands this in her bones. Ezekiel 16 begins with a baby who had no one to hold her at all.

Ezekiel was a priest who was carried off to Babylon in 597 BC with the first wave of exiles from Judah. Around him, the captives clung to the hope that Jerusalem could never fall, since it was the city God had chosen. Chapter 16 is God's answer to that confidence, and it is the longest single prophecy in the book. It pictures Jerusalem as a woman and retells her whole history as a love story that went terribly wrong. God tells Ezekiel to begin at the very beginning, with her birth, and even reminds the city that her roots were ordinary: "your father was an Amorite and your mother a Hittite" (Ezekiel 16:3).

Then comes the scene that makes this chapter unforgettable. "On the day you were born your cord was not cut, nor were you washed with water to make you clean, nor were you rubbed with salt or wrapped in cloths" (Ezekiel 16:4). In the ancient Near East these were the first small mercies given to every wanted child, and the custom of rubbing a newborn with salt lingered in parts of the Middle East into modern times. This baby received none of them. "No one looked on you with pity," God says, "rather, you were thrown out into the open field, for on the day you were born you were despised" (Ezekiel 16:5). She was left there in her own blood, still wet from birth, in a place where no one would hear her cry.

"Then I passed by and saw you kicking about in your blood, and as you lay there in your blood I said to you, 'Live!'" (Ezekiel 16:6)

In Hebrew the command is a single word, chayi, and God speaks it twice in the same verse, as if to make sure the child hears. He says it while she is still lying in her blood, before anyone has washed her or wrapped her. The story goes on with God raising her, and when she comes of age he spreads "the corner of my garment" over her and enters a marriage covenant with her (Ezekiel 16:8), the same gesture Ruth asked of Boaz on the threshing floor (Ruth 3:9). He bathes her, dresses her in embroidered cloth and fine linen, and sets a crown on her head. Her beauty becomes famous among the nations, God says, "because the splendor I had given you made your beauty perfect" (Ezekiel 16:14).

Then the heartbreak begins with one short line: "But you trusted in your beauty" (Ezekiel 16:15). What follows is written with a frankness that still makes readers uncomfortable, as she gives away her jewelry, her fine clothes and even her children to other lovers and other gods. Ezekiel is describing Jerusalem's idolatry and its anxious alliances with Egypt, Assyria and Babylon, and he refuses to soften any of it. Through all the grief, one phrase returns like a lament: "you did not remember the days of your youth, when you were naked and bare, kicking about in your blood" (Ezekiel 16:22; see also 16:43). Her ruin started with forgetting where she had come from and who had found her there.

That is why the ending of the chapter is so astonishing. After nearly sixty verses of judgment, God says, "Yet I will remember the covenant I made with you in the days of your youth, and I will establish an everlasting covenant with you" (Ezekiel 16:60). The Hebrew verb is zakar, and in Scripture, when God remembers someone, it rarely means he simply recalls a fact. It means he moves to act on their behalf, as when "God remembered Noah" and the floodwaters began to recede (Genesis 8:1). One way to read Ezekiel 16, then, is as a story about two memories. She let the field and the blood and the voice that said "Live!" slip away, and God kept every detail of that day.

The final verse carries the thought one step further. "Then, when I make atonement for you for all you have done, you will remember and be ashamed and never again open your mouth because of your humiliation, declares the Sovereign LORD" (Ezekiel 16:63). The word for atonement, kaphar, is often understood as covering, and the image fits the chapter beautifully. The God who once covered an abandoned girl with the corner of his garment covers her again, this time over her guilt. Only after that does she finally remember. Her shame in this verse is the hush of someone who has been forgiven far beyond anything she could explain, so she stops defending herself because grace has left her with nothing to argue.

Most of us live closer to this chapter than we would like to admit. We tend to remember our failures in vivid detail while the story of our rescue fades into a vague gratitude. When life becomes comfortable, with the promotion, the new house, or the children finally settled, it is easy to start trusting in our own beauty and to forget the season when we lay helpless and God passed by. The same forgetting quietly damages our human relationships, because we lose touch with the people who once held us when we were cold: the tita who paid our tuition, the friend who sat with us in the hospital, the parent who sent money home every month without complaint.

The love that found you before you could do anything is the same love that remembers you after you have done everything wrong. Tonight, before you sleep, you could take a few minutes to recall one specific field where God found you, perhaps a hospital bed, a year without work, or the season your family nearly fell apart, and thank him for it by name and in detail. Tomorrow, you might send a message to one person God used to hold you in that season and tell them you have not forgotten.

A cold newborn on its mother's chest does not have to warm itself before it is held, and it does not have to understand what is happening for the warmth to reach it. Ezekiel 16 ends with a God who reads our need the same way and answers it with an everlasting covenant. If you have wandered far from the field where he first found you, the word he spoke there still stands over your life, and it is the same single word: live.

articles.title: The Weight You Are Allowed to Lean
articles.dek: In a tense stretch of Psalm 119, the poet asks God for one thing: to be held up. The Hebrew word he uses shows how much of your weight God means to carry.
articles.quote: Faith, in the Hebrew of this psalm, looks like a tired person putting their full weight on God and finding that he holds.
articles.body:
In early 2009, Bob Chapman faced a problem that every business owner dreads. His company, Barry-Wehmiller, a maker of packaging and industrial machinery based in St. Louis, had watched its orders fall sharply as the global financial crisis spread. The numbers said what numbers usually say in a recession: cut people. Plenty of firms were doing exactly that, and no one would have blamed him for joining them.

Chapman chose a different road. Instead of laying off part of the workforce, he asked everyone in the company, from the factory floor to his own office, to take four weeks of unpaid furlough, scheduled however each person could best manage it. His reasoning, as he later told it in his book Everybody Matters, was simple: it was better for all of them to suffer a little than for some of them to suffer a lot. Then something happened that no spreadsheet had predicted. Employees who could afford it began volunteering to take extra weeks so that colleagues carrying heavier burdens could take fewer. The company came through the downturn, and people who had been bracing for a termination letter discovered that the place they worked would bear their weight.

For a Filipino reader, that story lands close to home. Many of us have lived through the season of the rumored retrenchment, the contract that might not be renewed, or the agency abroad that suddenly stops answering messages. What a person most wants to hear in that season is that someone stronger has decided to hold them up. That longing sits at the heart of today's reading.

Psalm 119 is the longest chapter in the Bible, an acrostic poem of 176 verses built on the twenty-two letters of the Hebrew alphabet. Each stanza has eight lines, and every line in a stanza begins with the same letter. Verses 113 to 120 belong to the letter samekh, and the writer, whose name we never learn, is clearly under pressure. He speaks of evildoers pressing close (v. 115), of people who stray from God and wicked people discarded like dross (vv. 118–119), and of his own body trembling before the Lord (v. 120). Somewhere in the middle of that pressure, he stops describing his enemies and simply asks for help.

"Sustain me, my God, according to your promise, and I will live; do not let my hopes be dashed. Uphold me, and I will be delivered; I will always have regard for your decrees." (Psalm 119:116–117)

The word translated "sustain" is the Hebrew verb samak, which echoes the very letter that opens the stanza, a touch of the poet's craft. Samak is a physical word. It describes leaning your weight on something, or bracing something so that it does not fall. In Leviticus, a worshipper bringing an offering was told, "You are to lay your hand on the head of the burnt offering" (Leviticus 1:4), and the verb there is the same one, carrying the sense of pressing down and resting one's weight.

That gives verse 116 a tender shape. The psalmist asks God to be the thing he leans on with his whole weight. Psalm 37:24 uses the same word for what God does for his people: "though he may stumble, he will not fall, for the LORD upholds him with his hand." The picture is of a hand under an arm, the way a grandchild helps a lola up the church steps, taking more of her weight with every step she climbs.

The first line of the stanza opens this further. "I hate double-minded people, but I love your law" (Psalm 119:113). The Hebrew word for "double-minded," se'aphim, is related to the word for a branch that splits off in two directions. Elijah used a close cousin of it on Mount Carmel when he asked the people of Israel, "How long will you waver between two opinions?" (1 Kings 18:21). Quite literally, he asked how long they would keep hobbling between two branches. A double-minded person keeps a foot on each limb, leaning a little on God and a little on whatever else might hold.

Read side by side, verses 113 and 116 form a quiet pair. The psalmist rejects the divided posture and asks for the leaning one. One way to read the whole stanza is as a man deciding where to put his weight. He has watched the wicked lean on their own cleverness, and he says that their "delusions come to nothing" (v. 118). He has chosen to rest the full load of his life on God's promise, and he admits that he cannot stand unless God holds him.

Isaiah gathered this same idea into one of Scripture's most loved promises: "You will keep in perfect peace those whose minds are steadfast, because they trust in you" (Isaiah 26:3). The word for "steadfast" there is samuk, a form of the same verb. A steadfast mind, in Isaiah's Hebrew, is a mind that is propped up, resting its weight on God. Peace comes to the person who has finally stopped trying to hold themselves up.

There is also a quiet honesty in the phrase "do not let my hopes be dashed." The Hebrew reads more literally, "do not let me be put to shame because of my hope." The psalmist knows that hoping in God is a public thing. People can see whom you are leaning on, and if that support gives way, you fall in front of everyone. He is asking God to honor the trust he has placed in him. Centuries later, Paul could answer that prayer with confidence: "hope does not put us to shame, because God's love has been poured out into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us" (Romans 5:5).

The employees at Barry-Wehmiller learned something about their company in 2009 that they could only have learned in a hard year. They found out whether the place to which they had given their working lives would carry them. The psalmist is praying for that same discovery about God, and he anchors his request in solid ground with the words "according to your promise." He leans on what God has already said, and he expects God to keep his word.

Most of us are better at holding ourselves up than we care to admit. We pray, and then we keep a backup plan in our pocket, a second branch to step onto in case God is slow. Some of that is ordinary prudence, and the Bible honors careful planning. Yet there are burdens that planning cannot lift, such as a hard diagnosis, a fresh grief, a child far from home, or a debt that keeps growing. For those, the psalmist offers a gentler posture, in which you name the weight plainly and ask God to take it.

Before the day ends, you might choose one specific load you have been carrying alone and pray verse 116 over it in your own words: "Sustain me, my God, according to your promise." Then find one promise to rest on, perhaps Isaiah 41:10, "I will strengthen you and help you; I will uphold you with my righteous right hand," and write it somewhere you will see it before you sleep. When the worry returns tomorrow, let it become a reminder to shift a little more of your weight onto him.

The stanza closes with the psalmist trembling in awe (v. 120), and that is a fitting place to end. Anyone who has leaned their whole weight on God and felt him hold knows the mixture of reverence and wonder in that moment. Faith, in the Hebrew of this psalm, looks like a tired person putting their full weight on God and finding that he holds. May you find that today, and may your hope never be put to shame.

articles.title: The Cord That Will Not Be Cut
articles.dek: A father in Proverbs warns his son against envy and excess, then hands him a Hebrew word that means both "hope" and "rope." It may be the most steadying promise in the whole book.
articles.quote: Your hope is a cord God himself is holding, and he has promised that no one will cut it.
articles.body:
On June 12, 2005, Steve Jobs stood before the graduating class of Stanford University and began simply: "Today I want to tell you three stories from my life." The first was about dropping out of Reed College after only six months. Free from required classes, he stayed around the campus and sat in on whatever interested him, including a course in calligraphy. He learned about serif and sans serif typefaces, about the spacing between letters, about what makes good lettering beautiful. None of it had the slightest practical use in his life at the time.

Ten years later, while he and his team were designing the first Macintosh computer, all of it came back to him. They built those lessons into the machine, and it became the first personal computer with beautiful typography. Then Jobs said the line that people still quote two decades later: "You can't connect the dots looking forward; you can only connect them looking backwards. So you have to trust that the dots will somehow connect in your future." The speech has since been watched tens of millions of times, and I suspect it endures because every one of us lives somewhere in the middle of an unfinished picture, holding dots that do not yet make sense.

Jobs told the graduates they had to trust in something, and he left that something open. About three thousand years earlier, a father in ancient Israel sat his son down and said much the same thing about the unfinished middle of life. The difference is that he named the One who holds the pencil.

Our passage comes from a section of Proverbs that begins at 22:17 and is introduced as "the sayings of the wise." It reads like a training manual, the kind of counsel an older official might give a young man preparing for life at court. Scholars have long pointed out that parts of this section resemble an Egyptian teaching text called the Instruction of Amenemope, which tells us something lovely: Israel's teachers gathered the best practical wisdom of their world and then set it firmly under the fear of the LORD. The young man being addressed would have been surrounded by people who seemed to be winning. Some had grown rich by cutting corners. Others threw lavish banquets where the wine never stopped and the meat kept coming. To a young person on a modest salary, those people looked like the future. The father sees it differently, and he says so.

"Do not let your heart envy sinners, but always be zealous for the fear of the LORD. There is surely a future hope for you, and your hope will not be cut off." (Proverbs 23:17–18)

Two Hebrew words in verse 18 carry the weight of the whole passage. The first is acharit, translated "future." It literally means the latter part of something, its ending, the place where a story finally lands. Envy almost always makes its judgments at the halfway mark. We see someone's harvest and compare it to our planting season, and the comparison feels crushing. The father is asking his son to measure lives by their acharit, by where they end up. The writer of Psalm 73 learned this the hard way. He confessed, "For I envied the arrogant when I saw the prosperity of the wicked" (Psalm 73:3), and his envy nearly made him give up on faith altogether. Relief came only when he went into God's presence: "till I entered the sanctuary of God; then I understood their final destiny" (Psalm 73:17). The phrase "final destiny" is that same word, acharit. Worship gave him back the long view.

The second word is tiqvah, translated "hope." It comes from a root that means to wait, and also to twist or bind together, and in at least one famous place it means a literal rope. When the spies told Rahab how her family would be saved from the fall of Jericho, they said, "tie this scarlet cord in the window" (Joshua 2:18). The word for that cord is tiqvah. One way to read Proverbs 23:18, then, is with Rahab's window in mind. Your hope is a cord God himself is holding, and he has promised that no one will cut it. The cord may run through seasons that look like nothing, like a calligraphy class with no apparent use, but it is tied to something solid at the other end.

That image also explains why the father moves so quickly from envy to the banquet table. In verses 19 to 21 he says, "Listen, my son, and be wise, and set your heart on the right path: Do not join those who drink too much wine or gorge themselves on meat, for drunkards and gluttons become poor, and drowsiness clothes them in rags." The connection is subtle and beautiful. People who believe they have no future tend to consume everything tonight. If there is no acharit worth waiting for, then the sensible thing is to drink the whole bottle and spend the whole paycheck. Excess is what hopelessness looks like at the dinner table. The father's final picture is almost comic in its sadness, a man so sleepy from last night's feast that he wakes up dressed in rags. He spent his tomorrow on his today.

Envy and excess, it turns out, grow from the same root. Both lose sight of the ending. The cure the father offers is to "always be zealous for the fear of the LORD," which means to keep a reverent, wholehearted awareness that God is real, present, and in charge of how the story ends. That steady awareness is what keeps a young heart from either resenting other people's banquets or trying to throw its own.

Centuries later, God spoke through Jeremiah to exiles who had lost nearly everything, and he used these same two Hebrew words side by side: "plans to give you hope and a future" (Jeremiah 29:11). In the original, that is tiqvah and acharit, the cord and the ending, promised together. And in the gospel, the promise takes on flesh. Peter writes that God "has given us new birth into a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead" (1 Peter 1:3). The cross looked like the place where every thread was finally severed. Three days later, God connected the darkest dot in history to the brightest one. If he could bring resurrection out of a sealed tomb, he can certainly bring meaning out of the season you are in right now.

For many of us, the pull of envy arrives through a phone screen. A batchmate posts the new house in Canada. A cousin is in Japan for the third time this year. A former officemate seems to have built a business overnight while you are still counting pesos before payday. In that moment, the father's voice in Proverbs gently asks you to remember that you are seeing someone else's middle chapter, and that your own story has an ending God has already secured. The pull of excess often follows close behind. It shows up as the payday splurge, the online bet, or the extra round with friends that we tell ourselves we deserve because life feels so hard. The same truth answers both temptations, because a person who knows their future is safe in God's hands has no need to grab at someone else's life or to swallow their own all at once.

When you feel envy rise today, you might take out a piece of paper and write down one dot that God has already connected in your past, a closed door that led somewhere better, a hard season that taught you something you now treasure. Then pray Proverbs 23:18 aloud as a promise addressed to you by name. Before your next payday, decide ahead of time what you will save and what you will give, so that your spending reflects a person with a future.

Steve Jobs was right that we cannot connect the dots looking forward. Scripture adds the good news he left unnamed: there is Someone who already sees the whole picture, and he has tied your life to his own risen Son. Hold on to that cord today. It is stronger than it looks, and it will not be cut.
